Augustine of Hippo lived from 354 to 430 CE and was an influential North African theologian and bishop whose ideas profoundly shaped Christian doctrine for over a thousand years. Originally a rhetor drawn to philosophy and sensual living, Augustine converted to Christianity through the influence of his mother and the preaching of Ambrose. He became one of Christianity's greatest theological minds. Born in Numidia, in what is now Algeria, to a pagan father and Christian mother, Augustine initially pursued philosophy and lived as a Manichean before his dramatic conversion. His book called the Confessions, written around 397 CE, ranks among history's earliest autobiographies, blending personal narrative with theological reflection on grace and redemption. Augustine taught that humans are bound by original sin—inherited moral corruption from Adam—and depend entirely on God's grace for salvation, not on human merit. He distinguished between the "City of God," the community of the elect destined for salvation, and the "City of Man," the earthly kingdom of secular ambition. His theology of predestination asserted that God foreknew and predetermined who would be saved, a claim that sparked centuries of debate over human free will and divine omniscience. As Bishop of Hippo in North Africa, he defended orthodox Christianity against several heresies, including Pelagianism, which denied original sin and overemphasized human moral capacity.
